records.place: Upper Moutere, the Moutere Hills, Nelson

wine.name: Neudorf Home Block Moutere Chardonnay
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, built on the Mendoza clone, which the house credits with the wine's firm acid and high extract.
wine.sites: The Home Block at Upper Moutere, planted in 1978 and among the first Chardonnay vines of the South Island, farmed organically and without irrigation for more than four decades on the clay gravels of the Moutere Hills.
wine.making: Fermented wholly in French oak barrels with wild yeast and a high share of solids, a small part of the oak new. The wine rests for some ten months on its full lees, stirred until the malolactic fermentation is done, then for a few months more on fine lees in stainless steel before bottling.
wine.glass: Lemon curd, white peach and lily over a note of home baking and pie crust, with a seam of oyster shell; firm acidity from the Mendoza clone and a fine, layered texture from the lees.
wine.ageing: Open on release, it is built on firm acidity and gains a savoury, nutty depth over several years in bottle; keep a strong vintage longer.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly if it seems tight; a wide white wine or Burgundy glass.

label.means: The block planted in 1978 beside the winery, the source of the original Moutere Chardonnay.
The Moutere Hills west of Nelson city, old clay soils threaded with gravel.
The wine region at the top of the South Island, on Tasman Bay.

records.table: Neudorf's Home Block Moutere Chardonnay comes from vines planted at Upper Moutere in 1978, dry farmed and organic on clay gravels. Wild fermented in barrel and raised on its lees, it gives lemon curd, white peach and pie crust over firm acidity.
records.story: In 1973 the Seifried family planted the first modern vineyard of the region at Upper Moutere, and three years later, in 1976, a young couple from the North Island moved into the Moutere Hills, buying a former commune property. In 1978 they planted their first vines there, Chardonnay among them, on the weathered clay gravels of the hills. That planting, the Home Block, is among the first Chardonnay of the South Island, and it rests on the Mendoza clone, which the house credits with the firm acid and high extract of its wine. The vines have never been irrigated, a rule the estate has kept for more than four decades, and the vineyards came to be farmed organically. For years the wine was sold simply as Moutere Chardonnay; the label later named the Home Block it comes from, and a second Chardonnay joined it from Rosie's Block, planted in 1999 and made the same way so that each site can speak. Pinot Noir and Riesling from the same hills complete the range. To a sommelier the Home Block wine is the white that first put Nelson's clay hills on the map of New Zealand Chardonnay, and the reference for what the Moutere gives.

traps: Home Block Moutere Chardonnay and the older label Moutere Chardonnay are one wine: the label added the block's name, it is not a new cuvée.
Moutere is a district of the Nelson region, not a separate appellation, and its clay gravel soils differ from the alluvial Waimea Plains near the city.

Fermented cool in steel and bottled within months

questions.exp: The Home Block went in in 1978; 1973 is the year of the Seifried family's first vineyard nearby, and 1999 the planting of Rosie's Block.

The region record's line that the wine gave Nelson a place among the country's best whites is a judgement; this record says it put the Moutere on the map of New Zealand Chardonnay.

wine.name: Seifried Winemakers Collection Sweet Agnes Riesling
wine.sites: In the vintages the house describes, the Edens Road vineyard, bordered by the Wairoa River, on markedly stony soil; the house picks from whichever of its estate vineyards gives the ripest fruit that year.
wine.making: Picked late and by hand, without botrytis, from grapes much of which have shrivelled and raisined on the vine by natural drying. The berries are pressed gently, and the concentrated juice ferments slowly before the young wine is stabilised and bottled early, within months of the harvest. It is not made in every year.
wine.glass: Apricot, honey and crystallised citrus peel, with orange marmalade in some years; very sweet and luscious, held in balance by tangy Riesling acidity.
wine.ageing: Delicious young for its fruit, it keeps its acidity well in bottle and gains a deeper, honeyed character with age.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass and a modest pour, with blue cheese or a fruit tart.

records.table: Sweet Agnes is Seifried Estate's sweet Riesling, named for the co-founder: picked late by hand from grapes raisined on the vine without botrytis, it tastes of apricot, honey and candied peel over tangy acidity. Pour it cold, in a small glass.
records.story: An Austrian born winemaker arrived in New Zealand in 1971 and there met his future wife, who had grown up on a Southland sheep farm. Together they bought land in the Moutere valley and in 1973 planted the first modern vineyard of the region, against the warnings of those who held that Nelson was too far south and too cold to ripen grapes. Their first vintage followed in 1976, sold from the cellar door at Upper Moutere. The family kept planting: the Redwood Valley vineyard, a north facing slope on solid Moutere clay, went in in 1979 and holds its oldest established vines, and later sites spread across the Waimea Plains. In 1998 the first vineyard of 1973 passed to new owners as Kahurangi Estate. Sweet Agnes, named for the co-founder, became the family's sweet Riesling, made only when the late autumn lets the grapes shrivel and concentrate on the vine without rot. In 2014 the Decanter World Wine Awards gave its 2012 vintage a regional trophy for New Zealand sweet wine. To a sommelier it is the wine that shows what the region's founding family does with Riesling, and a New World sweet wine made from raisined rather than botrytised grapes.

questions.exp: Sweet Agnes is picked late from grapes shrivelled and raisined by natural drying, with no botrytis; it is neither botrytised like a Trockenbeerenauslese nor made from frozen juice.

report: Pick in doubt as the plan says: Sweet Agnes is the house's most decorated wine and the one it is known by abroad, but it sits in the Winemakers Collection, not at the head of the Estate range; no swap is proposed.
The first release of Sweet Agnes in 2006 rests on the British importer's sales sheet alone, so the story gives no year for it.
The five grapes of the first vintage of 1976 (Riesling, Sylvaner, Chardonnay, Müller-Thurgau and Refosco) came in one search summary of unclear source and are left out.
One New Zealand Wine page gives 1996 as the inaugural vintage; it is read as the cellar door's opening, and 1976 stands on the house and Decanter.
Residual sugar runs from about 150 to about 200 grams a litre by vintage on the house's own pages, so no figure is given.
The founders are living and never named; the label's name Sweet Agnes stands as a label term.

records.place: Hope, on the Waimea Plains, Nelson

wine.name: Greenhough Hope Vineyard Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, built by the house's account on its oldest vines, of the clones UCD5 and AM 10/5, planted in 1993.
wine.sites: The home vineyard at Hope, inland on the Waimea Plains: clay rich loam and river stones over deep gravels laid down by the Wairoa River, the clay holding moisture; certified organic since 2011.
wine.making: Fermented with wild yeast, a share of whole bunches that changes with the vintage and the rest destemmed into open vessels, with few punch downs. The wine is raised for about a year in French oak barriques, a minority of them new, and bottled without fining or filtration.
wine.glass: Sliced strawberry and orange peel over a savoury edge and a spicy perfume; fragrant and elegantly built, medium bodied, with a dry, appetising backbone.
wine.ageing: Fragrant on release, it may close for a spell in its first years and opens again with more time in bottle; most vintages drink well within a decade.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle opens with half an hour of air; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The home vineyard of the house at Hope, on the inland edge of the Waimea Plains.
The wine region at the top of the South Island, on Tasman Bay.

records.table: Greenhough's Hope Vineyard Pinot Noir comes from the family's organic home vineyard on clay loam over river gravels at Hope. Wild fermented with some whole bunches and bottled unfined, it is fragrant and savoury, with strawberry, orange peel and a dry backbone.
records.story: The gravels of Hope were laid down some twenty thousand years ago, as the house tells it, when frost broke the eastern ranges and the floods of the Wairoa River spread loose stones across the plain; a finer clay loam in the upper soil sets this inland site apart from the stonier terraces nearer the sea. In late 1990 a young couple left Auckland for this rural pocket of Nelson to make wine, and their family estate took its name from them. Their oldest vines, the clones UCD5 and AM 10/5, went in in 1993 and became the core of the Hope Vineyard Pinot Noir, with a barrel fermented Chardonnay and a sweeter styled Riesling beside it. In 2008 the couple turned the home vineyard over to organic farming, and after the three year conversion it was certified by BioGro, the New Zealand organic body, in 2011. The Pinot Noir is wild fermented, partly with whole bunches, and bottled without fining or filtration. For a sommelier it is the Waimea Plains answer to the Pinot Noir of the Moutere Hills: a small, family made, organic red from the flat land near the city, fragrant and savoury rather than weighty.

records.place: Sunrise Road, Upper Moutere, the Moutere Hills, Nelson

wine.name: Kahurangi Estate Riesling
wine.sites: The home block near Upper Moutere village, first planted in 1973 by the Seifried family, whose Riesling vines the house describes as the oldest commercial Riesling of the South Island.
wine.making: The house publishes little of its cellar method for this wine. It is a single vineyard wine from the old vines of the home block, made in a dry or nearly dry style, with the touch of sweetness set by the vintage.
wine.glass: Lemon, lime and a flinty note on the nose, then grapefruit and green apple on the palate, with juicy acidity and a long finish; age brings a fuller, more complex texture.
wine.ageing: Fresh and citrus led when young, it gains texture and complexity with several years in bottle.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, with smoked fish or a light seafood dish.

records.table: Kahurangi Estate's Riesling comes from the home block at Upper Moutere, planted by the Seifried family in 1973 and, by the house's account, the oldest commercial Riesling of the South Island. Lemon, lime and flint, dry or nearly so, with juicy acidity.
records.story: The vineyard on Sunrise Road at Upper Moutere is where the modern wine of Nelson began. In 1973 the Seifried family planted the region's first modern vines here, on the clay soils of the Moutere Hills, against warnings that Nelson was too cold to ripen grapes, and three years later, in 1976, the family made its first vintage. As the Seifrieds planted elsewhere, the original site changed hands: in 1998 a new family bought it and renamed it Kahurangi Estate. The home block holds a mix of grapes, Chardonnay, Pinot Gris, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc and even Montepulciano among them, but its claim to note is its Riesling, which the house describes as the oldest commercial Riesling vines of the South Island. That claim is the house's and its stockists': Heaphy, a neighbour at Upper Moutere, claims an old Riesling block of its own, so the wine is safer told as Riesling from the vines of 1973. The house bottles a single vineyard Nelson Riesling and a Mt Arthur Reserve Riesling, and its range runs on to Estate Reserve and Regional Selection wines. For a sommelier it is the place to taste what half a century of Moutere Riesling vines give: a lean, citrus led white with real length.

Possible swap of wine: the Mt Arthur Reserve Riesling is the house's reserve bottling of the old vines and may be the truer flagship; not proposed without a second source.

records.place: The Bronte Peninsula above the Waimea Inlet, Moutere, Nelson

wine.name: Rimu Grove Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from several clones grown on the estate.
wine.sites: The estate vineyard, planted in 1995 on a gentle north facing slope of the Bronte Peninsula, a former orchard overlooking the Waimea Inlet, on clay and gravel soils of the Moutere.
wine.making: Picked by hand and cold soaked for some days before fermenting in small open vats, plunged by hand several times a day. The wine is aged in French oak barrels, for about ten months in some vintages and nearly two years in others, and bottled without fining or filtration.
wine.glass: Dark plum and sweet berry over bramble, mushroom and savoury spice; smooth and full, with juicy acidity, fine grained tannin and a long, graceful finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable within a few years of the vintage; the house has offered library vintages going back two decades, and age draws out its mushroom notes.
wine.serve: 14 to 16 degrees Celsius; no need to decant a young bottle, an old one gently off its sediment; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The winery's name, after the rimu, a native New Zealand conifer.
The wine region at the top of the South Island, on Tasman Bay.

records.table: Rimu Grove Pinot Noir is the estate red of a small winery planted in 1995 on a north facing slope above the Waimea Inlet. Hand plunged in open vats and bottled unfined, it gives plum, bramble and mushroom over fine grained tannin.
records.story: The vineyard of Rimu Grove lies on the Bronte Peninsula, a finger of the Moutere coast reaching into the Waimea Inlet west of Nelson city, on a gentle north facing slope that was once an orchard. In 1995 its founder, who had come to New Zealand from abroad, bought the site and planted it with Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris, making Pinot Noir the focus of the house. The estate Pinot Noir is made in the Burgundian manner: hand picked, cold soaked, fermented in small open vats plunged by hand, aged in French oak and bottled without fining or filtration. With the years the range grew around it: Bronte wines from the peninsula, a Pinot Noir called Synergy, and Pinot Noirs named for Mapua and for the view, while the winery's own bar became a place to taste them. Rimu Grove has also kept back older vintages, and its lists have offered Pinot Noir going back to the 2000 vintage, a rare chance to taste aged Nelson red. For a sommelier it is the coastal Moutere Pinot Noir to set beside the Chardonnay of the hills: a small, single estate wine whose savoury notes show what the Moutere clay gives to Pinot Noir with age.

report: Swap proposed: Rimu Grove is a small estate whose recent face is a bar and restaurant, its sources are thin and mostly its own, and it is not in the region record; Waimea Estates or Mahana should be researched as a fifth house a guest is likelier to know.
Founded 1995 rests on Glengarry, Grape to Glass and the house's own vineyard page; the Taste Nelson timeline alone gives 1980 and is not followed.
The oak time runs from ten to twenty two months across the vintage pages, so the making gives a range and no figure for new oak.
The Bronte wine is called Bronte Pinot Noir on some pages and a blend of Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Pinot Meunier on a drinks menu; the trap tells only what the menu says.
The rimu as the source of the name is general knowledge, not a sourced claim of the house; cut it if the checker wants a source.
The founder may be living and is never named.
